NDDR-CNN: Layer-wise Feature Fusing in Multi-Task CNN by Neural Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction

State-of-the-art Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) benefits a lot from multi-task learning (MTL), which learns multiple related tasks simultaneously to obtain shared or mutually related representations for different tasks. The most widely-used MTL CNN structure is based on an empirical or heuristic split on a specific layer (e.g., the last convolutional layer) to minimize different task-specific losses. However, this heuristic sharing/splitting strategy may be harmful to the final performance of one or multiple tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel CNN structure for MTL, which enables automatic feature fusing at every layer. Specifically, we first concatenate features from different tasks according to their channel dimension, and then formulate the feature fusing problem as discriminative dimensionality reduction. We show that this discriminative dimensionality reduction can be done by 1 [MATH \times] ×\times 1 Convolution, Batch Normalization, and Weight Decay in one CNN, which we refer to as Neural Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction (NDDR). We perform ablation analysis in details for different configurations in training the network. The experiments carried out on different network structures and different task sets demonstrate the promising performance and desirable generalizability of our proposed method.
1 Introduction

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have greatly pushed the previous limits of various computer vision tasks since the seminal work [20] in 2012. CNN models can naturally integrate hierarchical features and classifiers, which can be trained in an end-to-end manner. Benefiting from that, significant improvements have been witnessed in fundamental computer vision tasks, such as image classification [20, 45, 13, 16, 15], object detection [8, 7, 36, 12, 35, 25, 44, 48, 42, 43], semantic segmentation [4, 26, 37, 1, 33, 5, 2, 49, 3], etc.

One of the main factors that can further boost the CNN performance is multi-task learning (MTL), which learns multiple related tasks simultaneously. This is because related tasks can benefit from each other by jointly learning some shared, or more precisely, mutually related representations [12, 19]. The multiple supervision signals from different tasks in MTL can be viewed as implicit data augmentation (on labels) or additional regularization (among different tasks) [39]. This enables to learn mutually related representations that work well for multiple tasks, therefore avoiding overfitting and leading to better generalizability.

Most commonly, the CNN structure for MTL is heuristically determined by sharing all the convolutional layers, and splitting at the fully-connected layers for task-specific losses. However, as different layers learn low-, mid-, and high-level features [53], a natural question raises: Why would we assume that the low- and mid-level features for different tasks in MTL should be identical, especially when the tasks are loosely related? If not, is it optimal to share the features until the last convolutional layer?

This problem was also explored in a pioneer research [31], i.e., the cross-stitch network, in which the answer is negative: sharing/splitting at different layers gives different performance. Especially, improper features sharing at some network layers may degrade the performance of some, or even all, tasks. In addition, the deep nature of CNNs makes it infeasible to exhaustively test all the possible structures to find the optimal sharing/splitting. In order to tackle this, the cross-stitch network [31] used trainable scalars to weighted-sum the features from different tasks at multiple CNN levels and achieved the state-of-the-art performance.

We consider this problem in another way, i.e., by trying to utilize all the hierarchical features from different tasks. This is because different CNN layers trained by different tasks can be treated as different feature descriptors, and the features learned from them can be treated as different representations/views of the data. We hypothesize that these features, obtained from multiple feature descriptors (i.e., different CNN levels from multiple tasks), contain additional discriminative information of the data, which should be exploited in MTL for better performance.

Specifically, starting with [MATH K] KK single-task networks (from [MATH K] KK tasks), a direct attempt to take advantage of hierarchical features from all the tasks is that, we may concatenate all the features at layers of the same level from different tasks according to the feature channel dimension. After that, we expect the CNN to learn the task-specific feature embeddings by receiving these concatenated features as inputs. However, most existing CNNs have carefully designed structures, which only receive features (tensors) with fixed number of feature channels. By feature concentration, we in fact enlarge the number of channels as [MATH K] KK times if we have [MATH K] KK tasks. This makes it impossible to feed these concatenated features to the following layers of the CNN.

This property of the CNN motivates us to do discriminative dimensionality reduction on the concatenated features. This is to learn a discriminative feature embedding, and to reduce the feature dimension so that it can satisfy the input channel requirement of the following layers. Feature transformation is one of the most important approaches to tackle the discriminative dimension reduction problem. It aims to learn a projection matrix that projects the original high-dimensional feature into a low-dimensional representation, while keeping most discriminative information.

In this paper, we show that, from the feature transformation perspective, discriminative dimensionality reduction is closely related to some common operations of the modern CNNs. Specifically, the transformation in discriminative dimensionality reduction is in fact equivalent to the [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution. In addition, the constraints on the norm of the transformation weights (i.e., the weights of the [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolutional layer) and the input feature vectors can be represented by weight decay and batch normalization [17], respectively. We refer to the combination of these operations as Neural Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction (NDDR). Therefore, we are able to link the original single-task networks from different tasks by the NDDR layers. Desirably, the proposed network structure can be trained end-to-end in the CNN without any extraordinary operations.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. First, we detail the NDDR layer and propose a novel NDDR-CNN (and its variant NDDR-CNN-Shortcut) for MTL in Sect. 2. After that, we discuss the related works in Sect. 3, where we show that our method can generalize several state-of-the-art methods, which can be treated as our special cases. In Sect. 4, the ablation analysis is performed, where the hyper-parameters used in our network are suggested. Following that, the experiments are performed on different network structures and different task sets in Sect. 5, demonstrating the promising performance and desirable generalizability of our method. We make concluding remarks in Sect. 6.
2 The Proposed Method

In this section, we propose a novel method to automatically learn the optimal structure for layer-wise feature fusing in a multi-task CNN. Instead of the “split-style” multi-task CNN (e.g., split at the last convolutional layer for different task-specific losses), we consider the “fuse-style” network combining multiple single-task networks via discriminative dimensionality reduction.

We first relate the discriminative dimensionality reduction to [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution and propose the NDDR layer. Then, a novel multi-task network is proposed, namely NDDR-CNN, where the NDDR layer is leveraged to connect the original single-task networks. Moreover, a variant of NDDR-CNN is introduced, namely NDDR-CNN-Shortcut, which enables to directly route the gradients into the lower NDDR layers by shortcut connections. Finally, we give the implement details of the proposed network.
2.1 The NDDR Layer

As discussed in previous sections, we are aiming to utilize the hierarchical features learned from different tasks with the same single-task network structure. This is different from the most widely used method which heuristically shares all the low- (and mid-) level features and splits the network at the last convolutional layer.

In order to do that, we first concatenate the features of the layers at the same level from different tasks according to the channel dimension. Then, we use discriminative dimensionality reduction technique to reduce the feature channels so that the output feature satisfies the channel dimension requirement of the next CNN layers. We refer to the new CNN layer with such operations as the Neural Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction (NDDR) layer.

Specifically, let [MATH F^{i}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times W\times C}] Fli∈ℝN×H×W×CF^{i}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times W\times C} be the output feature (tensor) at an intermediate layer [MATH l] ll of task [MATH i] ii. Discriminative dimensionality reduction learns a transformation [MATH W] WW to reduce the dimensionality of the input features, while keeping most discriminative information:

where [MATH W\in\mathbb{R}^{KC\times M}] W∈ℝK​C×MW\in\mathbb{R}^{KC\times M} and [MATH M<KC] M<K​CM<KC. In our case, [MATH M] MM is equal to [MATH C] CC (i.e., [MATH F_{l}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times W\times C}] Fl∗∈ℝN×H×W×CF_{l}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times W\times C}) in order to satisfy the channel size requirement of the following CNN layers.

Conventional discriminative dimensionality reduction methods learn the transformation [MATH W] WW with specific assumptions/objectives which make the features more separable. For example, Linear Discriminative Analysis (LDA) learns [MATH W] WW by minimizing the projected within-class variation and maximizing the projected between-class variation [29]. Intuitively, the objective function of the discriminative dimensionality reduction is related to the CNN loss, i.e., the features projected by discriminative dimensionality reduction are more separable, therefore giving a smaller CNN loss.

Motivated by this, we aim to learn the transformation [MATH W] WW in the CNN implicitly by back-propagation. As shown in Fig. 1, the transformation [MATH W\in\mathbb{R}^{KC\times C}] W∈ℝK​C×CW\in\mathbb{R}^{KC\times C} can be represented precisely by a convolution operation with stride 1 and size ( [MATH C\times 1\times 1\times KC] C×1×1×K​CC\times 1\times 1\times KC), where these size dimensions represent filters, kernel height, kernel width, and channels, respectively. It is worth noting that the convolution with [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 kernel size and 1 stride enables to perform the computations only according to channels, rather than fusing the features at different spatial locations or changing the spatial size of the features.

In addition, discriminative dimensionality reduction methods also have constraints on the norms of the transformation [MATH W] WW (to avoid a trivial solution) and the input feature [MATH F_{l}] FlF_{l} (otherwise, the learned projection may project the features to some noise direction). We also borrow this idea to our NDDR layer for stable learning, which can be achieved by imposing batch normalization on the input features and [MATH \ell_{2}] ℓ2\ell_{2} weight decay on the [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolutional weights [MATH W] WW, respectively.

In summary, a novel NDDR layer is proposed in this section. The NDDR layer can be done by 1) concentrating the features at layers of the same level from different tasks according to the channel dimension, and 2) using [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution to reduce the feature channels. We also use batch normalization on the input features of the NDDR layer for stable learning. We train the NDDR layer by back-propagating the task-specific losses and the [MATH \ell_{2}] ℓ2\ell_{2} weight decay loss on the [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolutional weights [MATH W] WW. Without any extraordinary operations, the network with our NDDR layer can be trained end-to-end.
2.2 The NDDR-CNN Network

We insert the NDDR layers at multiple levels of the original single-task networks, to enable layer-wise feature fusing/embedding for different tasks. We refer to the proposed network for MTL as the NDDR-CNN network.

Figure 2 shows the NDDR-CNN network structure for two tasks. It can be easily extended to [MATH K] KK-task problems. Let the number of channels for the single-task features be [MATH D] DD. Then NDDR-CNN for [MATH K] KK tasks can be constructed by: 1) concentrating the features from [MATH K] KK tasks according to the channel dimension, and 2) use [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution with (filters [MATH \times 1\times 1\times] ×1×1×\times 1\times 1\times channels) = ( [MATH C\times 1\times 1\times KC] C×1×1×K​CC\times 1\times 1\times KC) to conduct dimensionality reduction, where [MATH C] CC is the channel dimension size of the output features from each task.
2.3 The NDDR-CNN Network with Shortcuts

In order to avoid gradient vanishing at lower NDDR layers, we propose a new network that enables to pass gradients directly from the last convolutional layer to the lower ones by shortcut connections, namely NDDR-CNN-Shortcut.

Specifically, the output of each NDDR layer is resized to the spatial size of the last convolutional output. Then we concatenate all the resized feature maps of the same task from different layers together according to the channel dimension. Finally, in order to fit the input size of the following fully-convolutional/connected layers, we further use [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution to learn more compact feature tensors (e.g., in the VGG network, we reduce the channels dimension of concatenated features to 512). An illustration of the NDDR-CNN-Shortcut network is shown in Fig. 3.
2.4 Implementation Details

Note that the state-of-the-art convolutional network architectures such as VGG [45], ResNet [13] and DenseNet [16] typically group similar operations into stages/blocks, where each stage contains {convolution-activation}n (possibly with pooling). In order to impose the least modification to the baseline network architecture to investigate the performance of the proposed NDDR layer, we only connect the two networks by applying the NDDR layer at the end of each stage/block. For example, for the VGG network, we apply the NDDR layers at the outputs of pool1, pool2, pool3, pool4 and pool5. Similarly, as much deeper as ResNet is, we still apply only 5 NDDR layer in it, e.g., at the outputs of conv1n3, conv2_3n3, conv3_4n3, conv4_6n3 and conv5_3n3 for ResNet-101.

In addition, as analyzed in the previous section, the input features need to be normalized before doing dimensionality reduction with NDDR layers. Therefore, we add the batch normalization (BN) layer between the convolutional layer and the ReLU layer that immediately before the NDDR layer. Note that by doing so, the input feature distribution to the following layers would change after inserting the NDDR layer and the BN layer. Thus, we add a BN layer after every convolutional layer for stable learning. This is extremely important for the networks originally without BN layers, such as AlexNet [20] or VGG-Net [45].
3 Related Works

Various computer vision tasks are benefited from MTL [41], such as detection [8, 7, 36, 12, 44, 48, 42, 43], human pose and semantic segmentation [50], surface normal, depth and semantic segmentation [6]. Several human face related tasks, including face landmark detection, attributes detection, such as smile and glasses, gender classification and face orientation, are studied in [47, 11, 34]. Yim et al. uses face alignment and reconstruction as auxiliary tasks for face recognition [52]. MTL on sequence data are also studied in [24]. Recently, Kokkinos proposed a UberNet which enables a great number of low-, mid-, and high-level vision tasks to be learned simultaneously [19].

CNN based MTL theory also greatly developed in recent years. Long and Wang proposed a deep relationship network to enable the feature sharing at the fully-connected layers [27]. Starting with a thin network, a top-down layer-wise widening method was proposed to automatically determine which layer to split [28]. Yang and Hospedales uses tensor decomposition at initialization to share the MTL weights [51]. The weights to combine the task-specific losses were also studied, and a Bayesian approach was proposed to predict these weights [18].

Our method is closely related to the cross-stitch network [31], which showed that the widely-used empirical/heuristic splitting at the last convolutional layer might be harmful to some specific tasks in MTL. In order to find the optimal network structure for MTL, the cross-stitch network [31] used trainable scalars to scale the features at layers of the same level from different tasks, and then added them together as new features. Our work is related to the cross-stitch network but has three major differences: 1) We have different motivations, i.e., our work is motivated by learning discriminative low-dimensional embeddings on the concatenated features from multiple tasks. 2) Our method can generalize the cross-stitch network, i.e., by fixing the off-diagonal of the projection matrix as 0, and only updating the diagonal elements with the same value. 3) We further propose a NDDR-CNN-Shortcut model, which further uses hierarchical features (at diff. CNN levels) for better training and convergence. Most recently, Ruder et al. [40] extended the cross-stitch network as the sluice network, which predefines several subspaces on the features from each task and learns the weights to fuse the features between different subspaces. However, the number of subspaces is fixed for each task, and the features can only be fused between the subspaces which contain multiple feature channels. Our method can also take the sluice network as a special case. In other words, by using the proposed NDDR layers, we can automatically determine how to fuse the features according to each channel.

Our method is also related to discriminative dimensionality reduction. The goal of discriminative dimensionality reduction techniques is to reduce the computational and storage costs, by embedding high-dimensional data into low-dimensional data by keeping most of the discriminative information. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is one of the most popular conventional discriminative dimensionality reduction methods, which aims to find the optimal projection matrix by maximizing the between-class variance and meanwhile minimizing the within-class variance [30]. In addition, Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) can also be viewed as discriminative dimensionality reduction [14].

Introduced by network in network [22], [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution has been widely used in many modern CNN architectures [46, 13, 16, 23]. For example, it was used in ResNet to reduce the number of weights to train, by producing a “bottleneck unit” [13]. [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution is also implemented in feature pyramid network to fuse hierarchical features (at different CNN levels) on a single task [23]. We use [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution in another way, i.e., we formulate the multi-task feature fusing as a discriminative dimensionality reduction problem, and use [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolution to learn the feature embeddings between different tasks.
4 Ablation Analysis

In this section, several ablations have been done to analyze NDDR-CNN. Two factors about the NDDR layers are analyzed, i.e., different [MATH 1\times 1] 1×11\times 1 convolutional weight initializations (Sect. 4.1), and the scales of “base” learning rate (i.e., the learning rate for the remaining network) to train the NDDR layers (Sect. 4.2). Finally, we also analyze which pretrained weights should be used as initialization, i.e., the weights trained by ImageNet or by the different single tasks. We use two-task problem here and in the following sections.
We use semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction for the ablation analysis. The configurations for this task set are detailed in the following.

Dataset. The NYU v2 dataset [32] is used for semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction. We use the official train/val splits which include 795 images for training and 654 images for validation. For semantic segmentation, the NYU v2 dataset contains 40 classes such as beds, cabinets, clothes, books [10]. The NYU v2 dataset also have pixel-level surface normal ground truths precomputed by the depth labeling [6, 32, 21]. Figure 4 illustrates an example image and its corresponding labels in the NYU v2 dataset.

Network Architecture. We use the state-of-the-art architecture for pixel level tasks, i.e., Deeplab [4], for both semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction. Deeplab is essentially a VGG or ResNet network backbone with atrous convolution with atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP). We do not implement Fully Connected CRFs or multi-scale inputs as they are not related to the NDDR layer we proposed. In other words, we are careful to stick closely to the proposed NDDR layer by using the same atrous convolution and ASPP for all the methods, so as to clearly see the effects of simply incorporating the NDDR layer. We use Deeplab-VGG-16 architecture in all the ablation analysis.

Losses. We use softmax cross-entropy loss for semantic segmentation. For surface normal prediction, we use [MATH \ell_{2}] ℓ2\ell_{2} regression loss after normalizing the normal vector of each pixel to have unit [MATH \ell_{2}] ℓ2\ell_{2} norm (i.e. this represents the angle direction). Therefore, our loss for surface normal prediction is also equivalent to the cosine loss.

Evaluation Metrics. The performance of the semantic segmentation is evaluated by mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy (PAcc). For surface normal estimation, we use Mean and Median angle distance of all the pixels for evaluation (the lower the better). In addition, we also use the metrics introduced by [6], which are the percentage of pixels that are within the angles of [MATH 11^{\circ},22.5^{\circ},30^{\circ}] 11∘,22.5∘,30∘11^{\circ},22.5^{\circ},30^{\circ} to the ground truth (the higher the better).

4.2 Learning Rates for The NDDR Layer

In this section, we discuss the learning rate for the NDDR layer. There are two main reasons to set a larger learning rate specifically for NDDR layer. First, as analyzed in Sect. 4.1, the NDDR-CNN becomes single-task networks if we set a very large weight (i.e., [MATH \alpha=1] α=1\alpha=1, much larger than the weights of perception convolutional layers) at the diagonal of [MATH W_{1}^{T}] W1TW_{1}^{T}. Therefore, we hypothesize that the magnitude of the NDDR layer weights should be larger, and therefore requiring larger learning rate. Second, larger learning rate for NDDR layers is necessary if we fine-tune the NDDR-CNN from the pretrained single-task networks.

Therefore, we analyze the proper learning rate for the NDDR layer as how many times it should be with respect to the base learning rate (for the remaining network excluding the NDDR layers). Table 2 shows the performance of using different learning rates for the NDDR layer. It verifies that larger learning rates should be applied for NDDR layers. In practice, we suggest to use larger than [MATH 10] 1010 times of the base learning rate for the NDDR layer.
4.3 Pretrained Weights for The Network Initialization

Two network initialization strategies can be applied. We may use the network weights pretrained on ImageNet. Or, we can choose the network weights pretrained with corresponding single tasks. The later strategy provides higher performance at the initial steps but have already met the saddle points in the single-task training.

The results with different pretrained models are summarized in Table 3, which shows that initializing the pretrained weights from single tasks performs better. The results suggested that by simply adding several NDDR layers, we have enlarged the capability of the original networks, which further enables to skip the previously existed saddle points.
5 Experiments

In this section, we perform various experiments on both different network structures and different task sets to demonstrate the promising performance and desirable generalizability of the proposed NDDR-CNN.

Specifically, VGG-16 [45] and ResNet-101 [13] have been used in our experiments. In addition, we also test our proposed NDDR-CNN-Shortcut with the VGG structure, where the gradients can be passed to the lower NDDR layers directly by the shortcut connections. This is able to further demonstrate the performance of the proposed NDDR layer. We refer to this network as VGG-16-Shortcut.

We choose very diverse task sets including both pixel-level labeling, i.e., semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction on scene images, and image-level classification, i.e., age and gender classification on human faces. The configuration for each task set is detailed in the following.

For evaluation, we train each task separately using the common single-task network architecture without NDDR layers as our single task baseline. The results from the most widely used heuristic multi-task network structure is performed as our multi-task baseline, where all the convolutional layers are shared and the split takes place after the last convolutional layer. Finally, we also compare our method with the state-of-the-art cross-stitch network [31], in which we apply the same number of cross-stitch layers at the same locations as our NDDR layers. For fair comparison, we use the best hyper-parameters suggested in [31] to train the cross-stitch network.
5.1 Semantic Segmentation and Surface Normal Prediction

In this section, we test our network on VGG-16, ResNet-101 and VGG-16-Shortcut to verify the desirable performance of the proposed network. In addition, by doing this, we further demonstrate the desirable generalizability of the proposed NDDR layers on different network architectures.
The configurations of the semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction, and the best hyper-parameters to train the network can be found in Sect. 4.
5.1.1 Experiments on The VGG-16 Network
In this section, we combine two VGG-16 networks by applying NDDR layer at the outputs of pool1, pool2, pool3, pool4 and pool5.

Table 4 shows the results on semantic segmentation and surface normal prediction using VGG-16 network. Though as simple as our method is, it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. For example, our method outperform the cross-stitch network by around 3.4% in “within 11.25∘” metric in surface normal prediction, and 1.7% for the both metrics in semantic segmentation. These results demonstrate the promising performance of our method.
5.1.2 Experiments on The ResNet-101 Network
We perform the NDDR layers in the ResNet-101 network, where the NDDR layers are only applied at the output of conv1n3, conv2_3n3, conv3_4n3, conv4_6n3 and conv5_3n3.

The results are shown in Table 5. It indicates that our method consistently outperforms the baseline and state-of-the-art results. Noted that comparing with the as deep as 101-layer network, we only slightly modified the ResNet-101 by adding five NDDR layers. This results further demonstrates effectiveness of the proposed NDDR layer.
5.1.3 Experiments on The VGG-16-Shortcut Network
We test the proposed NDDR-CNN-Shortcut with the VGG-16 structure, i.e., the VGG-16-Shortcut network to further validate our performance.

Compared with ResNet, the VGG-16-Shortcut network resembles more to DenseNet [16]. In VGG-16-Shortcut, the gradients can be passed to the lower NDDR layers by the direct and shortest shortcut connections, rather than by multiple shortcuts in ResNet-like networks where the gradients may still decay33 3 Note that we did not implement the ResNet-like shortcuts DenseNet. This is because that 1) the ResNet-like shortcuts in DenseNet is less related to the NDDR layer we proposed. Therefore, we carefully stitch to the factors that influence the NDDR layer to analysis it more clearly; 2) We have already demonstrated our performance in ResNet-101 in Sect. 5.1.2..

The evaluation results for VGG-16-Shortcut are shown in Table 6. Compared with the performance on the “vanilla” VGG-16 network (i.e., Table 4), the results of both the cross-stitch network and our method are improved in VGG-16-Shortcut. Especially, the improvements in our method is higher than that in our counterpart.

Table 6 shows that our method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Especially, our method outperform the cross-stitch network by around 4.8% for “within 11.25∘” metric in surface normal prediction, and 1.7%-1.8% for the two metrics in semantic segmentation.
5.2 Age Estimation and Gender Classification

Dataset. We use the IMDB-WIKI dataset [38] for this task set, which contains 460723 images collected from 20284 subjects. After filtering out the images with more than one faces and the images without age or gender labels, the remaining 187103 images from 12325 subjects are used to perform our experiments. These contain images for both genders, and for ages from 0 to 99. We randomly choose 24090 images from 2000 subjects for evaluation, and the remaining 163013 images from 10325 subjects are used for training. In the training set, we have sufficient samples for both male and female, but the training data for ages is imbalanced. Some image examples, with the gender and age statistics, are shown in Fig. 5.
Network Architecture. The VGG-16 network is used as the base network in this experiment. The NDDR layers are applied at the outputs of pool1, pool2, pool3, pool4 and pool5 of the VGG-16 network.
Losses. Motivated by [38], we treat both age and gender estimations as classification problems, i.e., 2-class and 100-class classifications. Softmax cross-entropy loss is used in both tasks.

Evaluation Metrics. Classification accuracy (Acc) is used to evaluate the gender classification. For age estimation, we follow the metric from [38]. 6 Conclusions

In this paper, we propose a novel CNN based MTL framework. Firstly, the features at layers of the same level from different tasks are concatenated. Then, we perform Neural Discriminative Dimensional Reduction (NDDR) on them to learn the task-specific feature embeddings, which also satisfy the input size of the following layers. We show a close relationship between CNN and discriminative dimensionality reduction, which enables to learn the NDDR projection (as well as other CNN weights) in an end-to-end fashion without additional extraordinary operations of a modern CNN. In addition, our method also generalizes several state-of-the-art researches on the CNN based MTL, such as the cross-stitch network [31].

We perform detailed ablation analysis on the hyper-parameters. The experiments carried out on various CNN structures and different task sets demonstrate the promising performance and the desirable generalizability of our method. An interesting future direction could be studying explicitly imposing the dimensionality reduction assumption/objective on the NDDR layer.
